So off to the range I go this morning with the Contender twins wearing 10" and 14" inch bull barrels and my 50 ladder loads I recently featured. The load was 14 through 16 grains of H-110 in .5 grain increments, 10 rounds each. The bullet was from Montana Bullet Works, 145 grain silhouette gas checked lead bore riders seated out as far as possible without exposing the top lube groove. CCI standard small rifle primers in reformed once fired Winchester NT 5.56 cases, never before fired in a 7TCU chamber, so they still had some taper and the 23 degree shoulder (what's left of it after necking up). So, I was fire forming brass as well as load testing with a never before used powder (by me, in this cartridge) which was less than ideal. I have worked with H-110 for many years, and she's a funny bitch. In the magnum revolvers, she's what you use if you want to duplicate the original factory specs as introduced. In those cartridges, you run it right up against the wall maximum loadings, never reducing. H-110 (and W-296, identical powder) has a stigma of causing detonations in revolvers if reduced much, and magnum primers are required. There's a reason it's nicknamed "Flammable Dirt". It burns super clean if you get it right, but miss the load by much and you have lots of unburnt powder, a stuck bullet and a gun full of unburned powder, or worse. It's all caused by that pesky cylinder gap that revolvers have (Nagants excepted) and there's a momentary drop in pressure as the bullet jumps the gap. Flammable Dirt needs pressure to burn completely, and if the primer and initial burning powder in the column isn't sufficient to maintain pressure past the gap, the flame either goes out and you get a stuck bullet in the bore, or the flame doesn't go completely out, the bullet stops in the bore and becomes an obstruction, then the remaining powder suddenly builds pressure and the gun kabooms.

This isn't an issue in a closed breach tube, a mini artillery piece. Nevertheless, the 7mm TCU is a true wildcat, never commercially loaded. You have to scrounge for new loads in dark corners, there's a lot of extrapolation involved when a component differs from scant published data. The closest published load using H-110 was for a 135 grain jacketed in fire formed cases (10% more capacity) so I based my starting loads of that, and loads for the AAC .300 using similar bullet weights.

In other words, I wasn't in Kansas anymore, and was wandering way the hell off the farm with nothing but instincts and experience to guide me. My plan was to shoot five rounds of 14 gr. in the 10", then five rounds in the 14" before moving up half a grain. All shooting was done off a bag using right handed Past shooting gloves on both hands.

I fired the first round in the 10" with my left hand, head turned away, pointed at the berm. The gun went bang and felt and sounded like it normally does with a known load. I pulled the case out, it was beautifully fireformed, very little if any soot around the mouth and shoulder, and the primer edge radius looked unchanged. The primer was still flush. I put the next four rounds into a nice group about 2" and every case looked great, and the recoil was about the same as my established loads. I switched to the 14" for the next five loads and the group was even tighter and the longer gun easier to shoot. I had pretty much the same results at 14.5 grains, but first noticed lube splatter on the paper from the 10" barrel. The primers from the 14" are kinda sorta starting to look a little flattened, but barely.

Then I stepped up to 15 grains of H-110. Only one out of five in the 10" even hit the paper. The 14" still shot a decent string, but two of the five primers are clearly flattened. My hand was not happy now, and I was flinching. I stopped, leaving 20 rounds unfired that I've got to pull down. But these 30 cases fire formed beautifully, not one split or crack. Annealing makes all the difference!

Long story short, I found a safe load for my favorite round using my favorite powder that I just so happen to have a keg of. I think 13.0 grains will be my load for fire forming, and 14.0 for formed cases.

TL;DR I didn't blow my hand off.
